nodes.title: Programming fundamentals
nodes.why: You need core coding concepts to write any backend logic.
checkpoints: Variables store values that can be read and modified throughout a program.
Control flow statements like if, for, and while determine which code runs.
Functions encapsulate reusable logic and can return results.
Scope determines where a variable or function is accessible, preventing name clashes.

nodes.title: Git version control
nodes.why: All code changes are tracked and shared using Git.
nodes.quote: Comfort with Git, including branches and pull requests.
checkpoints: A branch isolates work, allowing independent commits without affecting main.
Merging integrates changes from a branch into another, preserving history.
Pull requests show proposed commits and enable reviewers to comment before merging.
Merge conflicts arise when concurrent edits change the same part of a file, because Git lacks a resolution.

nodes.title: JavaScript fundamentals
nodes.why: Node.js runs JavaScript, so you need to understand its core language features.
checkpoints: Variables declared with const cannot be reassigned, while let allows later assignment.
Asynchronous functions return promises, enabling non‑blocking operations.
The event loop processes callbacks after the current call stack empties.
Objects inherit properties from their prototype, so missing properties are looked up the chain.

nodes.title: Node.js with TypeScript
nodes.why: The service code is written in TypeScript and executed on Node.js.
nodes.quote: Build and test REST API endpoints in TypeScript on Node.js.
checkpoints: TypeScript adds static types to JavaScript, catching mismatched assignments at compile time.
The tsc compiler transpiles .ts files to JavaScript that Node.js can execute.
Node.js uses a single thread with an event‑driven architecture for I/O.
Modules are imported using import/export syntax, and Node resolves them at runtime.

nodes.title: HTTP fundamentals
nodes.why: REST APIs communicate over HTTP, requiring knowledge of methods and status codes.
nodes.quote: A working understanding of HTTP: methods, status codes and how caching headers behave.
checkpoints: GET requests retrieve data without side effects, while POST creates new resources.
HTTP status 200 indicates success, while 404 signals a missing resource.
Cache‑Control headers like max‑age tell browsers how long a response may be cached.
Idempotent methods such as PUT can be repeated safely because the result remains the same.

nodes.title: REST API design
nodes.why: You will create endpoints that follow REST conventions for the scheduling product.
nodes.quote: Build and test REST API endpoints in TypeScript on Node.js.
checkpoints: Endpoints should use nouns for resources and HTTP verbs to indicate actions.
Path parameters identify specific resources, while query parameters filter or paginate results.
Responses should include appropriate status codes, such as 201 for a created record.
Statelessness means each request contains all information needed, so server does not store client context.

nodes.title: PostgreSQL database
nodes.why: The application stores invoices and payments in a PostgreSQL relational database.
nodes.quote: Design PostgreSQL tables, write migrations, and add indexes when queries slow down.
checkpoints: PostgreSQL stores data in tables with rows and columns.
Each table has a primary key that uniquely identifies its rows.
Foreign keys enforce referential integrity between related tables.
SQL statements are executed within a transaction, which can be committed or rolled back.

nodes.title: SQL query writing
nodes.why: You need to retrieve and aggregate data such as invoices and payments.
nodes.quote: Basic SQL, including joins and aggregates.
checkpoints: INNER JOIN returns rows with matching keys in both tables.
LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table, filling missing right columns with NULL.
GROUP BY groups rows to compute aggregates like SUM or COUNT per group.
HAVING filters groups after aggregation, unlike WHERE which filters rows before aggregation.

nodes.title: Database migrations
nodes.why: Schema changes are applied safely using migration scripts.
nodes.quote: Design PostgreSQL tables, write migrations, and add indexes when queries slow down.
checkpoints: A migration defines incremental changes like CREATE TABLE or ALTER COLUMN.
Migrations are run sequentially, ensuring the database schema matches application code.
Rollback steps revert the schema to the previous state if a migration fails.
Each migration is recorded in a schema history table, so duplicate runs are prevented.

nodes.title: Database indexing
nodes.why: Indexes speed up query reads that filter on indexed columns.
nodes.quote: add indexes when queries slow down.
checkpoints: An index stores column values in a sorted structure, enabling fast lookups.
Using an index reduces read latency because the database can locate rows without scanning the whole table.
Each insert or update must also modify the index, so writes become slower.
A missing index causes full table scans, which increase query time as data grows.

nodes.title: Database transactions
nodes.why: Transactions ensure related records are saved together, preventing partial data.
nodes.quote: Use transactions so that an invoice and its payment records are never left half saved.
checkpoints: A transaction groups multiple statements that either all commit or all roll back.
If an error occurs, the transaction is rolled back, reverting all changes.
Isolation levels control visibility of uncommitted data, preventing dirty reads.
Committing a transaction finalizes changes, making them visible to other sessions.

nodes.title: Automated testing
nodes.why: Tests verify each change works and catch regressions before deployment.
nodes.quote: Write automated tests with every change, and fix the bugs that your tests find.
checkpoints: Unit tests isolate a single function to assert its output for given inputs.
Test runners execute all test files and report failures, halting the build on errors.
Mocks replace external dependencies so tests run deterministically without network calls.
Code coverage measures which lines were executed during tests, exposing untested logic.

nodes.title: Logging and debugging
nodes.why: Analyzing logs helps identify production errors quickly.
nodes.quote: Review logs to trace production errors back to their cause.
checkpoints: Log entries include timestamps, severity levels, and messages that describe events.
Structured logs in JSON allow automated parsing and filtering.
Stack traces show the call sequence that led to an exception.
Correlation IDs link related log entries across services, so the origin of an error is traceable.

nodes.title: Authentication and input validation
nodes.why: The service must verify users and ensure data integrity before processing.
nodes.quote: Handle authentication and input validation carefully, because we store customer data.
checkpoints: Authentication verifies identity, typically by checking credentials against a user store.
Tokens such as JWT carry user claims and are validated on each request.
Input validation checks format and type, rejecting malformed data before it reaches business logic.
Failing validation returns a 400 status, preventing unsafe data from being processed.
